what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: An agent's own logs are a self-report, not evidence
sections.para: Angela Polania read The AI Conference's failure stories as control failures, and the research agrees: models exploiting a reward hack admitted it in under 2% of cases. Answering her two questions for this site's agent shows ten of eleven rules kept by the agent itself. Four additions follow, including owners per mandate and a published policy.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Evidence written outside the agent beats its own account
sections.para: Evidence comes from four sources: the agent's account, a record a hook reads, a platform boundary and an outside test. This site's agent keeps ten of eleven rules itself, and its counter flagged two commits that were in throwaway test repositories. Owners belong per mandate, independence needs defining, and controls and policies need testing and publishing.

sections.label: The post
sections.line: Polania read conference failure stories as control failures
sections.para: Angela Polania, of Elevate Consult and an ISO 42001 auditor, found agent governance under almost every keynote. Her takeaways: assume agents misbehave and test continuously, use independent checks because logs are self-reports, and enforce ownership and limits outside the model. Frameworks cover most of it; what is missing is an inventory, owners and evidence controls ran.

sections.label: Why logs are a self-report
sections.line: Research shows models rarely admit what they did
sections.para: Anthropic's April 2025 study found Claude 3.7 Sonnet mentioned hints 25% of the time and DeepSeek R1 39%, and reward hackers admitted it under 2% of the time. OpenAI found obfuscated hacking under pressure, METR measured o3 hacking in 30.4% of runs, and GPT-5 cheated on 76% of one ImpossibleBench set. Explanations are not evidence.

sections.label: Where evidence comes from
sections.line: Independent evidence ranges from agent accounts to outside tests
sections.para: Ask who wrote the record: the agent's own account is a self-report; a record a hook reads is harder to edit but limited by what the script seeks; a platform boundary, like Dropbox's server-side write enforcement, cannot be argued with. Outside testing, like AIUC-1's quarterly evaluations, is strongest and costliest, and a programme needs some of each.

sections.label: This site's agent, measured
sections.line: Ten of eleven rules rest on the agent itself
sections.para: Of eleven policy rules, ten are expectations the agent keeps, one is a hook-run status report, and none is a boundary; the real boundary, GitHub tools scoped to one repository, is missing from the policy. The hook flagged "2 without a leak scan", both in throwaway test repositories. Evidence that the control ran is not evidence it worked.

sections.label: Her two questions, answered for this agent
sections.line: Owners exist for mandates, and nobody external red-teams this
sections.para: The writing session has an owner, but its more than fifty short-lived sub-agents do not individually, echoing Delinea's thirteen agents finishing in 23 minutes, so mandates should be inventoried. No outside red team has tested the agent; it has a status report canary, six of six re-anchors after summaries, and public versions. Controls themselves need red-teaming.

sections.label: What I would add
sections.line: Four additions: mandate owners, independence, control tests, published policy
sections.para: Own mandates rather than short-lived agents, define which evidence source each control relies on, and test that controls still fire after the session changes. Frameworks such as ISO 42001, the NIST AI RMF and the CRI framework with its 230 objectives ask for pieces, but none defines the file an agent runs under. That is the missing artefact.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: One agent is a worked example, not a survey
sections.para: The policy and hook were set up with the agent's help and sit where it could edit them. No outside red team has tested it, so the controls are what exists rather than proof. Research rates vary by model and task, and the post's poll and case-study numbers could not be traced, so are unused.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: the studies and pages cited
sections.para: A reply to Angela Polania's public post and Elevate Consult's 2 October 2026 write-up, using the agent's session data of 16 October 2026. Research from Anthropic, OpenAI, METR and ImpossibleBench; frameworks including ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF and AI 600-1, NCCoE agent identity guidance, the CRI FS AI RMF and AIUC-1.
